recap_lines: Demographic parity, equalized odds and calibration parity are different tests.
With unequal base rates, the impossibility theorem says they cannot all hold.
Each metric carries a values claim, so the deliverable is a defended choice.
Individual fairness depends entirely on the similarity metric d.
Dropping a column is unawareness, and a proxy can bring the attribute back.
The GE Index splits total unfairness into within-group and between-group parts.
bookends.segment: Name The Metric, Rule Out Its Twin
bookends.command: Quiz me on fairness metrics. Give me one short case at a time, with made-up numbers for two groups. I must name the exact term, from demographic parity, equalized odds, calibration parity, base rate, proxy, individual fairness, direct effect and indirect effect, and say why its closest look-alike is wrong. Do not show the answer until I reply. After six cases, tell me which terms I mixed up.
checks: Check: Did each case make you name the exact term before the answer appeared?
Check: Did you explain why the look-alike term was wrong each time?

This film goes through the terms for that choice, each one shown.

beats.narration_text: A short proof in two bars. The impossibility theorem says that with unequal base rates, calibration parity and equalized odds cannot both hold. Equal precision forces the ratio of true-positive rate to false-positive rate to be two for Group A and seven for Group B. Equalized odds needs one ratio. For example, if more of one applicant pool is truly qualified, a hiring screen cannot keep its yes meaning the same in both pools and also make its mistakes at the same rates. One must give.
